Earth's Atmosphere.intro: The composition of Earth's atmosphere has changed dramatically over billions of years. Understanding this history is essential for C9.

sections.title: The Early Atmosphere
points: Formed by volcanic outgassing — volcanoes released gases from inside Earth
Mainly: carbon dioxide (CO₂), water vapour, nitrogen (N₂)
Very little or no oxygen (O₂)
Similar to current atmospheres of Mars and Venus

sections.title: How the Atmosphere Changed
numbered: Water vapour condensed as Earth cooled → formed oceans
CO₂ dissolved in oceans → reduced CO₂ levels; carbonates formed in rocks
Photosynthetic organisms (algae, plants) evolved → removed CO₂, released O₂
Oxygen levels gradually increased over billions of years
Nitrogen accumulated — unreactive, not removed by reactions
Ozone (O₃) layer formed from O₂ → absorbed UV radiation, allowed life on land

callout.label: Current Composition
callout.text: 78% nitrogen (N₂), 21% oxygen (O₂), ~0.9% argon (Ar), ~0.04% carbon dioxide (CO₂), variable water vapour.

keyTerms.def: Release of gases from volcanoes that formed Earth's early atmosphere
Process by which plants/algae used CO₂ and produced O₂ — changed the atmosphere
Layer of O₃ in the stratosphere that absorbs UV radiation

examTips: The key process that increased O₂: photosynthesis by early algae and plants.
CO₂ decreased because: dissolved in oceans AND used in photosynthesis.
Nitrogen built up because it is unreactive — not removed by any process.
commonMistakes: Saying nitrogen was produced by a specific process — it accumulated because it is unreactive.
Forgetting that CO₂ also dissolved in the oceans, not just used in photosynthesis.
clozePassages: The Earth's atmosphere is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 1% argon, and 0.04% carbon dioxide, along with water vapour and trace gases. This composition has been relatively stable for the last 200 million years. Early in Earth's history, the atmosphere was very different — mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour, with almost no oxygen. The current atmosphere developed through volcanic activity, condensation of water, photosynthesis, and the evolution of life.

The early atmosphere of Earth was dominated by volcanic gases including carbon dioxide, water vapour, and nitrogen. As the Earth cooled, water vapour condensed to form the oceans. Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and was used by marine organisms, gradually reducing its atmospheric concentration. The evolution of photosynthetic organisms produced oxygen, which accumulated in the atmosphere over billions of years, eventually reaching its current level of about 21%.

The current proportions of gases in the atmosphere are maintained by a balance of processes. Photosynthesis removes CO₂ and produces O₂. Respiration and combustion consume O₂ and produce CO₂. The nitrogen cycle involves bacteria converting nitrogen between different forms. Human activities — particularly burning fossil fuels — are disrupting this balance by adding extra carbon dioxide to the atmosphere faster than natural processes can absorb it.

Greenhouse Effect.intro: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere, keeping Earth warm enough for life. Human activities are enhancing this effect, causing climate change.

sections.title: How the Greenhouse Effect Works
points: Short-wave solar radiation passes through the atmosphere to Earth's surface
Earth absorbs it and re-emits as long-wave infrared radiation
Greenhouse gases absorb this infrared — re-emit in all directions
Net effect: heat is trapped, warming the atmosphere

sections.title: Greenhouse Gases
points: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) — burning fossil fuels, deforestation
Methane (CH₄) — livestock (digestion), landfill, rice paddies, natural gas leaks
Water vapour (H₂O) — natural; increases as temperature rises
Nitrous oxide (N₂O) — fertilisers, agriculture

sections.title: Climate Change Consequences
points: Rising average global temperatures
Melting ice caps and glaciers → rising sea levels
More extreme weather events (floods, droughts, storms)
Changing distribution of species
Disruption to agriculture and food security

keyTerms.def: Natural process where greenhouse gases trap infrared radiation, warming Earth
Increased warming due to human-caused rise in greenhouse gas concentrations
Long-term changes in global climate patterns due to enhanced greenhouse effect

examTips: The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life — the enhanced effect is the problem.
Methane is more potent than CO₂ as a greenhouse gas per molecule.
Be able to evaluate evidence for climate change — scientific consensus is overwhelming.
commonMistakes: Confusing the ozone hole (separate issue) with the greenhouse effect.
Saying the greenhouse effect is entirely man-made — it is a natural process that is being enhanced.
clozePassages: The greenhouse effect is the trapping of heat energy by certain gases in the atmosphere. The main greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour, and nitrous oxide. These gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface and re-emit it in all directions, warming the planet. Without any greenhouse effect, Earth's average temperature would be about -18°C. The enhanced greenhouse effect from human activities is causing climate change.

Human activities are increasing the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide. Deforestation reduces the amount of CO₂ removed by photosynthesis. Agriculture, particularly livestock farming, produces methane through digestion and decomposition of manure. Rice paddies and landfill also produce methane. Nitrous oxide is released from fertilisers. These increases are causing the planet to warm.

The scientific evidence for human-caused climate change is overwhelming. Ice core data shows that atmospheric CO₂ levels are higher now than at any point in the past 800,000 years. Global average temperatures have risen by approximately 1°C since pre-industrial times. The consequences include rising sea levels, more extreme weather, changes in species distribution, and food and water shortages. International agreements such as the Paris Agreement aim to limit warming to 1.5°C.

Air Pollution.intro: Burning fossil fuels releases pollutant gases that damage health and the environment. Understanding sources, effects and solutions is required for C9.

sections.title: Pollutants from Combustion
points: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) — greenhouse gas; from complete combustion of fossil fuels
Carbon monoxide (CO) — toxic; from incomplete combustion; binds to haemoglobin preventing O₂ transport
Soot/particulates — from incomplete combustion; cause respiratory problems; global dimming
Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) — from sulfur impurities in fuels; dissolves in rainwater → sulfuric acid → acid rain
Nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) — N₂ + O₂ at high engine temperatures; → acid rain and photochemical smog

sections.title: Effects of Pollutants
points: Acid rain: lowers pH of lakes (kills fish), erodes limestone buildings and statues, damages trees
Carbon monoxide: binds to haemoglobin → reduces O₂ in blood → suffocation at high concentrations
Particulates: respiratory problems, asthma, reduced sunlight (global dimming)

sections.title: Solutions
points: Catalytic converters in cars: convert CO and NOₓ to CO₂ and N₂
Flue gas desulfurisation: removes SO₂ from power station emissions using calcium oxide
Switching to low-sulfur fuels
Renewable energy to replace fossil fuels

keyTerms.def: Toxic gas from incomplete combustion — binds to haemoglobin
Acidic gas from burning sulfur-containing fuels — causes acid rain
Rain with lower than normal pH caused by SO₂ and NOₓ dissolving in water
Device in car exhaust that converts CO and NOₓ to CO₂ and N₂

examTips: CO is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin — prevents oxygen transport.
SO₂ + H₂O → sulfurous/sulfuric acid → acid rain.
Catalytic converters reduce CO and NOₓ — they do NOT reduce CO₂.
commonMistakes: Saying catalytic converters reduce CO₂ — they convert CO and NOₓ but produce CO₂.
Confusing CO (toxic, colourless) with CO₂ (not directly toxic at normal concentrations).
clozePassages: Carbon monoxide is a toxic gas produced by incomplete combustion of fuels in car engines and gas appliances. It is colourless and odourless, making it difficult to detect. It binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells more strongly than oxygen, preventing oxygen transport and causing suffocation. Catalytic converters in car exhausts convert carbon monoxide to carbon dioxide by oxidation over a platinum catalyst.

Sulfur dioxide is produced when fuels containing sulfur impurities are burned. It dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain, which damages buildings, kills trees, and acidifies lakes and rivers. Nitrogen oxides form in hot car engines when nitrogen and oxygen in the air react at high temperatures. They also contribute to acid rain and the formation of photochemical smog. Low-sulfur fuels and catalytic converters help reduce these pollutants.

Particulate matter from combustion and industrial processes contributes to air pollution. Fine particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and cause respiratory and cardiovascular problems. Carbon particles (soot) produced by incomplete combustion absorb heat and contribute to climate change when they settle on ice and snow. Reducing air pollution requires cleaner fuels, better emission controls, and a shift away from fossil fuels towards renewable energy sources.
